site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Prince Who Chose Kindness
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Five princes journeyed through a sun-warmed forest until thirst drew them to a shining pond, where a water-sprite dwelled among the lily stems. Four brothers rushed to drink without heed and were seized, leaving only the youngest to face the spirit alone.

The sprite posed riddles, and the prince answered each one with patient thought, his calm wisdom pleasing the guardian of the pool. Offered the freedom of a single brother, the prince did not choose the strongest or cleverest, but the one who had once been kindest to him.

Touched by such grateful love, the water-sprite released all four captives at once. The five princes walked onward together through the dappled forest, their bonds unbroken and their hearts renewed by grace.

stories.title: The Net Lifted Together
stories.source: Panchatantra · Book 2, The Winning of Friends
body: A flock of pigeons was caught in a hunter's net, their wings tangled and the sky suddenly out of reach. Their king spoke with calm urgency, telling them to stop struggling one by one and instead fly as one. Together they lifted the mesh on beating wings and carried it across the countryside toward a small burrow where help waited.

There lived Hiranyaka the mouse, a humble friend of the pigeon king, quick of paw and loyal of heart. When the flock arrived, he set to gnawing the cords with tireless patience. The king asked that every companion be freed before him, and Hiranyaka honored that wish, freeing each bird in turn before finally cutting the last knot around his royal friend.

So pigeons and a small gray mouse shared a quiet moment of grace at the mouth of a burrow, the net lying useless behind them. Their flight to him, and his patient teeth, became the beginning of a friendship across differences, a gentle promise that even the unlikely can lift one another free.

stories.title: A Moonlit Promise for the Rabbits
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: During a long drought, a thirsty herd of elephants trampled down the warrens of a small rabbit colony as they came to drink at their lake. The rabbit king, watching his people's homes crumble beneath great feet, chose cleverness over panic and called for a wise messenger to be sent to the elephant king.

That brave rabbit bowed before the elephant king and told him the lake belonged to the Moon itself, and that the god of the night sky was angered by the destruction of his tiny worshippers. He led the elephants back at nightfall, where the trembling reflection of the moon shimmered on the water's surface, and the elephant king, awed by what he saw, lowered his great head in apology.

Promising never to disturb the rabbits again, the herd turned away from the shore, and the small creatures kept their homes in peace. In that gentle exchange of reverence and wit, even the smallest voice was heard, and the lake belonged once more to the rabbits and the moon above it.

stories.title: Kanakadas and the Udupi Window
body: When the Kannada poet-saint Kanakadas came to the Udupi Krishna temple, the doors were closed to him because of his place in society. He did not turn away in anger; he settled near the back wall and lifted his voice in song, asking only for a glimpse of Krishna.

Even as he sang, the murti of Krishna within the sanctum turned, and a small opening appeared in the stone wall where Kanakadas waited. Through that unexpected window, called the Kanakana Kindi, the saint received the darshan his heart had longed for, offered freely by the divine.

The temple still remembers that moment: devotion, not birth or status, was what opened the way. Kanakadas returned home with his sight of Krishna, and the kindness of a turned face and a broken wall remains a gentle promise.

stories.title: The Geese Who Returned Home
stories.source: Mahahamsa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. V, H. T. Francis translation (public domain)
body: When Queen Khema dreamed of golden geese preaching wisdom beside a quiet lake, King Samyama ordered the waters made ready to welcome them. Soon the great golden Goose King and his loyal commander Sumukha glided down to bathe among the blossoms. It was there, in that peaceful place, that a fowler's snare caught the king by the wing.

Sumukha would not desert his leader, and so both were carried before the royal court. Yet when the king and queen heard Sumukha's steadfast devotion and the Goose King's gentle teaching on wise and compassionate rule, their hearts softened. They opened their hands and set the two birds free instead of keeping them captive.

The golden geese rose into the bright sky and winged their way home, where their flock greeted them with joyful cries. The whole company praised King Samyama, the fowler, and faithful Sumukha, for what began in a snare had ended in mercy, friendship, and the safe return of two wise hearts.
